subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 6! In this unit you will master two of the most useful ideas in all of mathematics: fractions and percentages. Both are ways of describing part of a whole. When Amina eats half of an anjero, when Yusuf scores 85% on a test, or when Halima sees a 30% off sign at the Hargeisa market, they are all using these very ideas. Fractions and percentages are everywhere, and by the end of this unit you will handle them with real confidence.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Identify and use proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers, and convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers.
Understand a fraction as division and connect it to its decimal value.
Use a fraction as an operator to find a fraction of a quantity (remembering that “of” means multiply).
Make and recognise equivalent fractions and simplify a fraction to its lowest terms.
Understand a percentage as a fraction out of 100, and calculate a percentage of an amount using several methods.
Work out percentage increases and decreases, and find an original amount after a change.
Convert freely between fractions, decimals and percentages and recognise common equivalents.
Solve multi-step word problems and interpret data given as fractions and percentages.
Compare and order fractions with different denominators, including where one denominator is not a multiple of the other, by converting to a common denominator.
Find a percentage of a shape by counting shaded parts out of a total number of equal parts, converting to a fraction out of 100 where needed.

concepts.title: Understanding Fractions
concepts.explanation:
A fraction is a way of writing part of a whole or part of a group. When Omar cuts a mango tart into 8 equal slices and eats 3 of them, he has eaten 3/8 (three-eighths) of the tart. A fraction has two parts. The numerator (top number) tells you how many parts you have. The denominator (bottom number) tells you how many equal parts the whole is divided into.

The line between them means divide. So 3/4 also means 3 ÷ 4. This is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit, and we will come back to it. First, let us meet the three types of fraction you must recognise.

Proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers

A proper fraction has a numerator smaller than its denominator, so it is less than one whole. Examples: 1/2, 3/4, 5/8, 7/10. If you have 3/4 of a chocolate bar, you have less than a full bar.

An improper fraction has a numerator equal to or larger than its denominator, so it is one whole or more. Examples: 5/4, 7/3, 9/5, 8/8. Do not let the name worry you – there is nothing wrong with these fractions. Eating 5/4 of a sambusa means one whole sambusa plus another quarter.

A mixed number joins a whole number with a proper fraction, such as 1 1/2, 2 3/4 or 5 2/3. If Farah runs 2 1/2 kilometres, she has run two whole kilometres and half of another.

Improper fractions and mixed numbers are simply two ways of writing the same amount. Being able to switch between them makes you flexible, so let us learn both conversions carefully.

Converting an improper fraction to a mixed number

Because the fraction bar means divide, you divide the numerator by the denominator. The whole-number part of the answer becomes your whole number; the remainder becomes the new numerator; and you keep the same denominator.

Example: Convert 11/4. Work out 11 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 3. So the whole number is 2, the remainder 3 is the new numerator, and the denominator stays 4. Therefore 11/4 = 2 3/4.

Converting a mixed number to an improper fraction

Do the reverse. Multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator. Write that total over the original denominator.
concepts.example: Example: Convert 3 2/5. Work out 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 + 2 = 17. Keep the denominator 5. Therefore 3 2/5 = 17/5.

concepts.title: A Fraction Is a Division
concepts.explanation:
Every fraction is secretly a division problem. The fraction 3/4 means 3 ÷ 4, which equals 0.75 as a decimal. This one idea explains a great deal:

It shows why 4/4 = 1, because 4 ÷ 4 = 1. Any fraction where the top and bottom are equal makes one whole.

It shows why a bigger denominator means smaller pieces. 1/8 is smaller than 1/4 because you are sharing the whole between more people, so each share is tinier.

It connects fractions to real sharing. If Hassan shares 3 dates equally among 4 children, each child gets 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4 of a date.

Because a fraction is a division, you can always turn it into a decimal by dividing the top by the bottom. This is exactly how we will later convert fractions into percentages. Keep this idea close – it ties the whole unit together.
concepts.example: Here is a useful way to picture it. Imagine 3 loaves of anjero shared equally among 4 members of a family. If you cut each loaf into 4 equal quarters, you have 12 quarters in all, and each person receives 3 of them – that is 3/4 of a loaf each. Notice that 3 ÷ 4 gives exactly the same answer as the fraction 3/4, and both equal 0.75. The sharing story, the division, the fraction and the decimal are four descriptions of a single idea. When you truly see this, fractions stop being mysterious symbols and become a natural, everyday way of splitting things fairly.

concepts.title: Fractions as Operators – Finding a Fraction of an Amount
concepts.explanation:
A fraction can also act as an operator, meaning it tells you to do something to a number. When we say “find 3/4 of 20”, the fraction 3/4 is operating on 20. In mathematics, the word “of” almost always means multiply, so “3/4 of 20” means 3/4 × 20.

There are two reliable methods, and both give the same answer. Choose whichever keeps the numbers friendly.

Multiply first, then divide: multiply the amount by the numerator, then divide by the denominator.

Divide first, then multiply: divide the amount by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator.

Example – find 3/4 of 20. Method 1: (20 × 3) ÷ 4 = 60 ÷ 4 = 15. Method 2: (20 ÷ 4) × 3 = 5 × 3 = 15. Both roads reach 15. Method 2 is often easier because dividing first keeps the numbers small.

Always add the correct units to your answer and estimate to check it is sensible. Here are three worked examples with different kinds of quantity:

Money: find 2/5 of 300 shillings. (300 ÷ 5) × 2 = 60 × 2 = 120 shillings. Check: 2/5 is less than a half, and half of 300 is 150, so 120 is reasonable.

Time: find 3/4 of 60 minutes. (60 ÷ 4) × 3 = 15 × 3 = 45 minutes. Check: 3/4 is close to a whole, so the answer should be close to 60.

Distance: find 5/8 of 24 km. (24 ÷ 8) × 5 = 3 × 5 = 15 km. Check: 5/8 is a bit more than a half, and half of 24 is 12, so 15 fits.
concepts.example: Sometimes you must compare fractions of different amounts. Work out each one separately, then compare the results. For example, who swims farther: Halima who swims 3/5 of 500 m, or Zahra who swims 2/3 of 600 m? Halima swims (500 ÷ 5) × 3 = 300 m. Zahra swims (600 ÷ 3) × 2 = 400 m. So Zahra swims farther, even though 2/3 and 3/5 look close, because the amounts they act on are different.

concepts.title: Equivalent Fractions and Simplifying
concepts.explanation:
Equivalent fractions are different fractions that describe the same amount. Just as “half”, “50%” and “0.5” all name the same quantity, the fractions 1/2, 2/4, 3/6 and 4/8 are all equal. Picture half a mango tart cut into 2, 4, 6 or 8 pieces – the amount you take stays the same even though the number of pieces changes.

To make an equivalent fraction, multiply the numerator and denominator by the same number:

To simplify (or reduce) a fraction, do the opposite: divide the top and bottom by the same number until you cannot go any further. This gives the fraction in its lowest terms. For example, 18/24: both numbers divide by 6, so 18/24 = (18÷6)/(24÷6) = 3/4. Simplifying makes fractions easier to read and compare.
concepts.example: Equivalent fractions matter for four big reasons: they let you add and subtract fractions with different denominators, they let you simplify answers, they help you recognise when two different-looking fractions are really equal, and they are essential for comparing fractions fairly. You will use them constantly.

concepts.title: Understanding Percentages
concepts.explanation:
A percentage is a special fraction whose denominator is always 100. The word “per cent” literally means “per hundred” or “out of 100”. So 25% means 25 out of 100, or 25/100, which simplifies to 1/4.

Percentages are useful because they give a standard way to compare. It is hard to compare 3/4 with 7/10 at a glance, but as percentages they become 75% and 70%, and now it is obvious that 3/4 is larger. Because every percentage is out of the same number, 100, comparisons become quick and fair. That is why test scores, discounts, statistics and interest rates are so often given as percentages.

Percentages also appear in ways you may not have noticed. A weather forecast that says there is a 30% chance of rain is really saying 30 out of every 100 similar days had rain. A pie chart of favourite sports at Nuur Academy uses percentages so that all the slices add up neatly to 100%. When a shopkeeper in Berbera marks up prices, works out profit, or offers a discount, every one of those steps is a percentage. Because they are everywhere, becoming confident with percentages gives you a kind of superpower for reading and judging the world around you – you can quickly tell whether a claim, a price or a score is as good as it first appears.

concepts.title: Calculating a Percentage of an Amount
concepts.explanation: There are three good methods for finding a percentage of an amount. Learn all three, then choose the easiest one for each problem. Since a percentage is a fraction out of 100, turn it into a simple fraction and use it as an operator. Find 20% of 150: 20% = 20/100 = 1/5, and 1/5 of 150 = 150 ÷ 5 = 30. The same idea works for finding a percentage of a shape, not just a percentage of a number. If a grid or a bar is divided into 100 equal small squares, then the number of shaded squares out of 100 is exactly the percentage that is shaded — 40 shaded squares out of 100 means 40% is shaded. If the grid has a different total number of equal parts, first work out what fraction is shaded, then convert that fraction to a percentage. For a shape divided into 20 equal parts with 7 shaded, the shaded fraction is 7/20, and since 7/20 = 35/100, the shape is 35% shaded.
concepts.example: Because 10% is just divide by 10, you can build other percentages from it. Find 30% of 80: 10% of 80 = 8, and 30% = 3 × 10%, so 30% of 80 = 3 × 8 = 24. Find 15% of 200: 10% of 200 = 20, and 5% is half of that = 10, so 15% = 20 + 10 = 30.

concepts.title: Comparing and Ordering Fractions with Different Denominators
concepts.explanation: When two fractions have the same denominator, comparing them is easy: just compare the numerators, since the pieces are the same size. For example, 5/8 is bigger than 3/8 because 5 eighths is more than 3 eighths of the same-sized pieces. The challenge comes when the denominators are different, because the 'pieces' are different sizes and cannot be compared directly. To compare fractions with different denominators, first rewrite them as equivalent fractions that share a common denominator — a number that both original denominators divide into evenly. A safe common denominator is always the product of the two denominators (multiply them together), though the lowest common multiple of the denominators gives smaller, easier numbers to work with. Once both fractions have the same denominator, compare the numerators exactly as before. This works even when the denominators are not multiples of one another, such as comparing 2/3 and 3/5, where neither 3 nor 5 divides evenly into the other, so you must find a shared multiple such as 15.
concepts.example: Compare 2/3 and 3/5. The denominators 3 and 5 share no common factor, so use their product: 3 × 5 = 15. Convert 2/3 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 5: 10/15. Convert 3/5 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 3: 9/15. Now compare 10/15 and 9/15: since 10 is greater than 9, 2/3 is greater than 3/5. To put three fractions in order, convert them all to the same common denominator first: ordering 1/2, 3/8 and 2/3 using twenty-fourths gives 12/24, 9/24 and 16/24, so the order from smallest to largest is 3/8 < 1/2 < 2/3.

methods.title: Convert an improper fraction to a mixed number
steps: Divide the numerator by the denominator.
The whole-number answer is the whole number.
The remainder becomes the new numerator.
Keep the same denominator. (17/4 = 4 1/4.)

methods.title: Convert a fraction to a percentage
steps: Divide the numerator by the denominator to get a decimal.
Multiply the decimal by 100.
Add the % symbol. (3/5 = 0.6 = 60%.)

methods.title: Simplify a fraction
steps: Find a number that divides both top and bottom.
Divide both by that number.
Repeat until no number bigger than 1 divides both. (18/24 = 3/4.)

methods.title: Percentage of an amount
steps: Build from 10%.
Then 5% is half of that = 4.
So 15% = 8 + 4 = 12 shillings.

methods.title: What percentage is one number of another?
methods.example: Sahra answered 16 out of 20 questions correctly. What percentage did she score?
steps: Write the smaller number over the larger number as a fraction.
Divide the numerator by the denominator to get a decimal.
Multiply the decimal by 100 and add the % sign.

workedExamples.title: Convert an improper fraction
workedExamples.solution: 17 ÷ 4 = 4 remainder 1. The whole number is 4, the remainder 1 is the new numerator, and the denominator stays 4. So 17/4 = 4 1/4.

workedExamples.title: Find a fraction of an amount
workedExamples.solution: Divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. 18 ÷ 3 = 6, and 6 × 2 = 12 mangoes. Check: 2/3 is more than a half, and half of 18 is 9, so 12 is sensible.

workedExamples.title: Simplify a fraction
workedExamples.solution: Both 18 and 24 divide by 6. 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4, so 18/24 = 3/4. There is no number bigger than 1 that divides both 3 and 4, so it is fully simplified.

workedExamples.title: Percentage of an amount
workedExamples.solution: Build from 10%. 10% of 80 = 8. Then 5% is half of that = 4. So 15% = 8 + 4 = 12 shillings.

workedExamples.title: What percentage is one number of another?
workedExamples.prompt: Sahra answered 16 out of 20 questions correctly. What percentage did she score?
workedExamples.solution: Write part over whole, then multiply by 100. (16 ÷ 20) × 100 = 0.8 × 100 = 80%.

workedExamples.title: A discount problem
workedExamples.prompt: A bicycle costs 150 shillings and is reduced by 20%. What is the sale price?
workedExamples.solution: A 20% discount means you pay 80% of the price. 80% of 150 = (80 ÷ 100) × 150 = 0.8 × 150 = 120 shillings. (Check the long way: 20% of 150 = 30, and 150 − 30 = 120. ✓)

workedExamples.title: A percentage increase
workedExamples.prompt: A young papaya tree is 20 cm tall. In one month it grows by 25%. How tall is it now?
workedExamples.solution: The increase is 25% of 20 = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm. New height = 20 + 5 = 25 cm.

workedExamples.title: Find the original amount
workedExamples.prompt: 60% of a number is 48. What is the number, and what is 75% of it?

workedExamples.title: A multi-step mixed problem
workedExamples.prompt: In a bag of 40 marbles, 1/4 are red, 30% are blue, and the rest are green. How many of each colour?

workedExamples.title: What percentage is
workedExamples.prompt: What percentage is: a) 16 out of 20 b) 12 out of 48 c) 24 out of 30?

workedExamples.title: Comparing a Fraction and a Percentage of an Amount
workedExamples.prompt: Which is larger: 3/4 of 80 or 60% of 100? Show your calculations.

activities.title: Kitchen Fraction Detective
activities.materials: a recipe (for anjero, bariis or a cake), measuring cups or spoons, paper and a pencil.
steps: Write down every fractional measurement in the recipe, such as 1/2 cup or 3/4 teaspoon.
Convert any mixed numbers (like 1 1/2 cups) into improper fractions.
Work out the amounts for half the recipe and for double the recipe.
Order all the measurements from smallest to largest to make a fraction chart.
Cooking is one of the most natural places to see fractions doing real work.

activities.title: Percentage Grid Art
activities.materials: grid paper with a 10×10 square (100 small squares), and coloured pencils.
steps: Plan a picture where each colour is a set percentage: for example 40% blue sky, 30% green grass, 20% brown trunk, 10% yellow sun.
Work out the exact number of small squares for each colour (remember, the whole grid is 100 squares).
Colour your design, keeping to your plan.
Check that all your percentages add up to 100% and all your squares add up to 100.
This shows how a percentage is simply a count out of 100.

activities.title: The Discount Shopping Game
activities.materials: old store flyers or handwritten price cards, and a pencil.
steps: Give each item a price and a percentage discount (for example 200 shillings, 25% off).
Work out the discount amount and the final price for each item.
Use the shortcut too: for 25% off, find 75% of the price in one step, and check it matches.
Compare two deals – which one truly saves more money?
You are training to be a smart shopper who can never be fooled by a sale sign.

activities.title: Sports Statistics Analyst (Investigation)
activities.materials: results from a football match or a shooting game you play, and a pencil.
steps: Record attempts and successes, for example 15 shots taken and 12 scored.
Write the success rate as a fraction, then simplify it (12/15 = 4/5).
Convert the fraction to a percentage (4/5 = 80%).
Compare two players or two matches and decide who was more accurate, explaining how you know.
This is exactly how real sports analysts compare performances fairly.

activities.title: Family Budget Pie (Group Task)
activities.materials: a pretend monthly amount (say 1,000 shillings) and paper for a circle chart.
steps: As a family (or with your AI tutor if you are working alone), decide how to split the money by percentage: for example 40% food, 20% school, 15% transport, 15% savings, 10% charity/sadaqah.
Work out the actual amount for each part.
Draw a pie chart, making each slice roughly match its percentage of the circle.
Check that all the percentages add up to 100% and the amounts add up to the total.
Sharing wisely and giving in charity (sadaqah) can be any amount you choose – planning it with percentages helps the whole family see the picture.

activities.title: Conversion Snap
activities.materials: small cards. On each, write a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.
steps: Make matching sets, such as 1/2, 0.5 and 50%, for several common values.
Shuffle all the cards and deal them out between two players — if nobody is available, use your AI tutor as your opponent instead.
Take turns laying a card face up; shout “Snap!” when two cards on the table are equal in value.
The player who spots the most correct matches wins.
Playing this a few times will fix the common equivalents firmly in your memory.

rules.title: Finding a Fraction of an Amount
rules.text: Fraction of an Amount “Of” means multiply. Divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. 3/4 of 20 = (20 ÷ 4) × 3 = 15.

rules.title: Finding a Percentage of an Amount
rules.text: Percentage of an Amount A percentage is a fraction out of 100. Method: (amount × percentage) ÷ 100. 35% of 120 = (120 × 35) ÷ 100 = 42.

rules.title: Percentage Increase and Decrease
rules.text: Increase and Decrease For a discount of 25%, you pay 75% of the price. For an increase of 10%, the new price is 110% of the old. To find the original, divide by the new percentage as a decimal.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: There are three good methods for finding a percentage of an amount. Learn all three, then choose the easiest one for each problem. Since a percentage is a fraction out of 100, turn it into a simple fraction and use it as an operator. Find 20% of 150: 20% = 20/100 = 1/5, and 1/5 of 150 = 150 ÷ 5 = 30.

selfAssessment: I can identify and use proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers, and convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers.
I can understand a fraction as division and connect it to its decimal value.
I can use a fraction as an operator to find a fraction of a quantity (remembering that “of” means multiply).
I can make and recognise equivalent fractions and simplify a fraction to its lowest terms.
I can understand a percentage as a fraction out of 100, and calculate a percentage of an amount using several methods.
I can work out percentage increases and decreases, and find an original amount after a change.
I can convert freely between fractions, decimals and percentages and recognise common equivalents.
I can solve multi-step word problems and interpret data given as fractions and percentages.
